WHY DID THE US PUT THESE FIVE COUNTRIES ON ITS AI CHIP WATCHLIST? 🇺🇸
🇸🇬 Singapore
🇲🇾 Malaysia
🇹🇭 Thailand
🇮🇩 Indonesia
🇧🇷 Brazil
Five countries, five different economies, and now one common concern from Washington: Who is actually getting access to advanced American AI chips?
On 16 November 2026, the US Commerce Department announced tighter export controls on advanced AI semiconductors, including additional licensing requirements for these five countries.
And no, this doesn't mean all five countries are banned from buying NVIDIA chips.
The rules are a little more complicated than that. 😂
FIRST, WHAT EXACTLY IS THE US RESTRICTING?
There are three important numbers and conditions:
1. 12 MILLION TPP
Data centres providing more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) to companies headquartered in restricted jurisdictions, including China, may trigger additional licensing requirements.
Even computing capacity across linked data centres can be counted together.
Importantly, this is a remote-computing threshold, NOT a blanket exemption for chip shipments below 12 million TPP to the five named countries.
2. 90 DAYS
Certain existing remote-computing arrangements will have 90 days from the effective date to obtain the required licence if they wish to continue operating.
3. US-HEADQUARTERED EXCEPTION
Certain shipments to US-headquartered companies, or companies with US-headquartered ultimate parents, are excluded from the new five-country licensing requirement, provided the required reporting conditions are met.
So the rules don't necessarily affect every operator equally.
BUT WHY THESE FIVE COUNTRIES?
Here's where their different roles in the AI industry matter.
🇸🇬 SINGAPORE — THE REGIONAL TECHNOLOGY & TRADING HUB
Singapore is a major centre for cloud services, semiconductor trading and regional technology operations.
Its role in cross-border technology supply chains makes chip movements and end-user verification particularly relevant.
The challenge? Maintaining its reputation as a trusted technology hub while navigating tighter US export controls.
🇲🇾 MALAYSIA — THE FAST-GROWING DATA CENTRE DESTINATION
Malaysia has attracted substantial data centre investment commitments, particularly around Johor.
The country is positioning itself as a regional destination for cloud and AI infrastructure.
But attracting investment is one thing. Ensuring operators can access advanced chips and serve compliant customers is another.
🇹🇭 THAILAND — THE EMERGING DATA CENTRE COMPETITOR
Thailand has been actively attracting cloud and data centre investments from international technology companies.
With different investors, operators and customer structures, additional licensing requirements could affect projects differently.
The question is whether regulatory procedures will influence future investment decisions and deployment timelines.
🇮🇩 INDONESIA — THE DOMESTIC DIGITAL ECONOMY
Indonesia has a large domestic market supporting demand for cloud computing, digital services and AI infrastructure.
Unlike facilities designed primarily to serve overseas computing customers, some Indonesian data centres focus on domestic demand.
That distinction could matter when assessing exposure to remote-computing restrictions.
🇧🇷 BRAZIL — LATIN AMERICA'S AI INFRASTRUCTURE AMBITION
Brazil is working to attract data centre investments through its energy advantages and investment incentives.
But cheaper infrastructure and favourable tax policies don't automatically guarantee access to the most advanced AI chips.
US export licensing could become another consideration for developers assessing new projects.
SO WHY DID WASHINGTON GROUP THEM TOGETHER?
According to the US Commerce Department, these five countries present a higher-than-normal risk of advanced semiconductor diversion.
The concern is that companies in restricted jurisdictions could access American computing technology through third countries.
Think about it.
A Chinese company might not be able to import certain advanced NVIDIA chips directly.
But what if it rents computing power from a data centre located overseas?
The chips never enter China.
The computing power can still be accessed remotely.
That's precisely the type of arrangement Washington is trying to control.
MY VIEW
I wouldn't interpret this as the end of AI infrastructure growth in these five countries.
But I do think it reveals something about the future of the AI industry.
Singapore is strengthening its position as a technology hub.
Malaysia is attracting data centre investments.
Thailand is competing for international infrastructure projects.
Indonesia is building capacity for its domestic digital economy.
Brazil wants to become a stronger AI infrastructure destination in Latin America.
Five different ambitions.
Yet access to some of the most advanced computing technology remains heavily influenced by US export policy.
And the implications won't necessarily be equal.
A US-linked hyperscaler, an independent GPU cloud provider and a data centre construction company can face very different commercial and regulatory exposures.
Having the land, electricity and billions in investment doesn't necessarily mean you control access to the technology.
Everyone wants a piece of the AI boom.
Apparently, Washington would also like to check the guest list. 😂
One final detail: The rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on 19 November 2026 and is not yet effective as of 17 November.
Sources: US Department of Commerce / Bureau of Industry and Security (16 November 2026), Federal Register public inspection copy, Reuters.

In Indonesia, the First Question Is What You Will Build Here

In most Asian markets the first serious question a customer asks is about the product. In Indonesia it is often about you.

What will you build here? Who will you employ? Where is your stock? Who is your partner, and do they have engineers or only salespeople?

It took me a while to stop hearing that as a negotiation tactic. It is policy, and it runs deep.

Indonesia has used local content requirements for years. It has pushed downstream processing of its own resources, from nickel to palm oil. Its B50 biodiesel programme, mandatory since July, keeps more of its palm oil inside its own fuel system. The direction is consistent: add the value in Indonesia.

For a European supplier of process equipment, plastics machinery or biofuel technology, that changes the entry plan. Exporting a machine and flying in for commissioning works once. To stay, you need a local assembly or service partner, a parts stock in the country, and a clear story about which part of your value is created in Indonesia.

That costs more upfront. It also explains why the suppliers who made that commitment years ago are so hard to dislodge.

This week Plastics and Rubber Indonesia runs in Jakarta. Walk the halls and notice who has a local team on the stand, not just a distributor's banner.

If you sell into Indonesia, what did you have to build locally before the business took off?

The global AI race talks in gigawatts and do-everything models. But Indonesia’s real needs are more specific: models for fisheries, agriculture, disaster response, healthcare, logistics, and regional financial services. These models don’t need one 1 GW campus. They need capacity that is close, resilient, and efficient.
That is the gap we are targeting: the middle layer between edge AI (small, on-site) and giant AI data centers (distant, expensive, generic).
The design: 140 data centers at 10 MW each. Each site has 4 buildings × 2.5 MW, with roughly 100 GPU racks per building. The network totals about 1.4 GW, but spread out, so each site can be built quickly and sit close to its sector’s data.
Why sector-specific learning?
Sector models are smaller, cheaper to train, and more accurate in their domain.
Sensitive data (health, finance, disaster) can stay in its home region.
One site is enough for fine-tuning and inference, with no queueing behind giant clusters.
No Kubernetes complexity
We treat each 2.5 MW building as a self-contained cluster, with fixed partitions per sector and a simple batch scheduler. Fewer layers, fewer things to break, and regional teams can actually operate it.
Key design features (from our feasibility simulator)
Zero water. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling in a closed loop, a karst-rock borefield, and dry coolers. WUE = 0 L/kWh, 0 L/year operating water use. In simulation, GPU junction temperature is about 77 °C (limit 85 °C) and PUE is about 1.02.
Megathrust-resistant, and affordable. A flexible steel frame in the Japanese style, allowed to sway and be damped, on a standard foundation. Only the server hall sits on an ISO-BASE (ball-n-cone) isolation floor. The heaviest equipment (generators, transformers, batteries) goes in a semi-basement to lower the center of gravity.
Near-fault resilience. In a near-fault scenario, standard isolation isn’t enough. Small modifications (parallel dampers, a wider cone, a longer stroke) turn the simulation result from fail to pass on firm ground.
Coastal corrosion resistance. Facade and interior are assessed against ISO 9223, with positive-pressure server halls.
An honest note: all figures come from a feasibility-level simulator, not a final engineering design. Results on soft soil are still marginal, and borehole-to-borehole interference and vendor data must be verified by licensed engineers. Simulation can be seen athttps://lnkd.in/gghm9_uV
My question for you: which sector in Indonesia is most ready to have its own AI model?

Hiring a Foreign Employee in Indonesia: What Happens Before Day One

In most countries, hiring someone from abroad starts with a work visa. In Indonesia, it starts one step earlier.

Before any visa, the employer needs approval from the Ministry of Manpower to use a foreign worker in that specific role. That approval, the RPTKA, sets the position and the period of employment. Everything else follows from it.

The usual order looks like this:

RPTKA approval for the role
Payment of the foreign worker compensation fund (US$100 per month, paid in advance for the planned period)
Work visa application, usually while the person is still outside Indonesia
Stay permit (KITAS) after arrival

Only then can the person start work. Coming in on a visit visa and sorting out the paperwork later isn’t an option.

A few things that often catch companies off guard:
→ Some positions are closed to foreigners, including a list of HR and personnel roles
→ A foreign hire generally needs a named Indonesian counterpart, with a plan for passing on skills
→ The details in the original application need to stay consistent, or renewals can be rejected
→ The sponsor has to be an Indonesian legal entity

That last point is where plans often stall. No local company means no one to apply.
An Employer of Record can fill that gap. We act as the Indonesian employer, run the permit process, and take care of contracts, payroll and social security once the person starts.

Plan for several weeks from application to start date, and begin before the offer letter goes out.

posts.text:
In Indonesia, the First Question Is What You Will Build Here

In most Asian markets the first serious question a customer asks is about the product. In Indonesia it is often about you.

What will you build here? Who will you employ? Where is your stock? Who is your partner, and do they have engineers or only salespeople?

It took me a while to stop hearing that as a negotiation tactic. It is policy, and it runs deep.

Indonesia has used local content requirements for years. It has pushed downstream processing of its own resources, from nickel to palm oil. Its B50 biodiesel programme, mandatory since July, keeps more of its palm oil inside its own fuel system. The direction is consistent: add the value in Indonesia.

For a European supplier of process equipment, plastics machinery or biofuel technology, that changes the entry plan. Exporting a machine and flying in for commissioning works once. To stay, you need a local assembly or service partner, a parts stock in the country, and a clear story about which part of your value is created in Indonesia.

That costs more upfront. It also explains why the suppliers who made that commitment years ago are so hard to dislodge.

This week Plastics and Rubber Indonesia runs in Jakarta. Walk the halls and notice who has a local team on the stand, not just a distributor's banner.

If you sell into Indonesia, what did you have to build locally before the business took off?

#CapitalRecycling via REITs (DIRE). Local telecommunications firms (likeTelkom Indonesia ) and developers carry heavy debt to build DC.
